cards.front: Name the seven major digestive functions.
cards.back: Ingestion, mechanical processing, chemical digestion, secretion, absorption, compaction, defecation.

cards.front: How is mechanical processing different from chemical digestion?
cards.back: It breaks food into smaller pieces without breaking chemical bonds.

cards.front: What is the difference between a bolus and chyme?
cards.back: Bolus is chewed, saliva-coated food; chyme is stomach-mixed semifluid.

cards.front: What happens during absorption?
cards.back: Nutrients, water, or ions cross GI epithelium into blood or lymph.

cards.front: How do catabolism and anabolism differ?
cards.back: Catabolism breaks down molecules; anabolism builds larger molecules.

cards.front: Why is pancreas called an accessory digestive organ?
cards.back: It secretes into the gut, but food does not pass through it.

cards.front: How do motility and compaction differ?
cards.back: Motility mixes or propels contents; compaction removes water and concentrates feces.

cards.front: List the four basic GI wall layers from lumen outward.
cards.back: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa/adventitia.

cards.front: Where is the myenteric plexus, and what does it regulate?
cards.back: Between muscularis layers; mainly motility.

cards.front: What does the submucosal plexus regulate?
cards.back: Secretion and local blood flow.

cards.front: Peristalsis versus segmentation: what is the main difference?
cards.back: Peristalsis propels; segmentation mixes.

cards.front: What are mass movements?
cards.back: Strong, infrequent colon contractions moving fecal material toward rectum.

cards.front: What is a mesentery?
cards.back: Double peritoneal sheet supporting organs and carrying vessels/nerves.

cards.front: Visceral versus parietal peritoneum?
cards.back: Visceral covers organs; parietal lines abdominal wall.

cards.front: What does retroperitoneal mean?
cards.back: Located behind the parietal peritoneum; much of pancreas is an example.

cards.front: Which salivary components lubricate and protect the mouth?
cards.back: Mucins lubricate; lysozyme and IgA contribute to defense.

cards.front: Which enzyme starts starch breakdown in saliva?
cards.back: Salivary amylase.

cards.front: Which salivary gland uses Stensen's duct?
cards.back: Parotid gland.

cards.front: Which salivary gland uses Wharton's duct?
cards.back: Submandibular gland.

cards.front: Where is the sublingual gland?
cards.back: Beneath the tongue, in the mouth floor.

cards.front: What is the fauces?
cards.back: Opening from oral cavity to oropharynx.

cards.front: Enamel versus cementum: what does each cover?
cards.back: Enamel covers crown; cementum covers root.

cards.front: What lies inside the tooth's pulp cavity?
cards.back: Blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue.

cards.front: What is the apical foramen?
cards.back: Root-tip opening for vessels and nerves.

cards.front: How many deciduous and permanent teeth are typical?
cards.back: 20 primary; up to 32 permanent.

cards.front: What are the three phases of deglutition?
cards.back: Buccal (voluntary), pharyngeal (involuntary), esophageal (involuntary).

cards.front: Which brainstem area helps coordinate swallowing?
cards.back: Medulla oblongata.

cards.front: What protects the airway during the pharyngeal phase?
cards.back: Laryngeal elevation/closure, with epiglottic assistance.

cards.front: How can food pass down the esophagus against gravity?
cards.back: Esophageal peristalsis.

cards.front: Which esophageal sphincter helps prevent acid reflux?
cards.back: Lower esophageal sphincter (LES).

cards.front: Which pharyngeal section is air-only?
cards.back: Nasopharynx.

cards.front: What is the esophageal hiatus?
cards.back: Diaphragm opening for the esophagus.

cards.front: What are the four stomach regions?
cards.back: Cardia, fundus, body, pylorus.

cards.front: Parietal cells secrete which two substances?
cards.back: Hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.

cards.front: Chief cells secrete which digestive substances?
cards.back: Pepsinogen and gastric lipase.

cards.front: What does hydrochloric acid do in the stomach?
cards.back: Supports denaturation, pepsin activation, and microbial killing.

cards.front: Why is pepsinogen secreted in inactive form?
cards.back: It limits proteolytic damage to the producing tissue.

cards.front: Why is intrinsic factor important?
cards.back: It is needed for efficient B12 absorption in terminal ileum.

cards.front: How does stomach mucosa resist its own acid?
cards.back: Mucus, bicarbonate, epithelial integrity, and repair.

cards.front: What are rugae?
cards.back: Expandable folds in the stomach lining.

cards.front: Which additional muscle layer aids gastric churning?
cards.back: Oblique smooth-muscle layer.

cards.front: What does the pyloric sphincter regulate?
cards.back: Chyme passage from stomach into duodenum.

cards.front: What triggers the cephalic phase?
cards.back: Sight, smell, taste, or thought of food.

cards.front: What triggers the gastric phase?
cards.back: Stomach stretching and food/peptides in its lumen.

cards.front: What is the main intestinal-phase feedback effect?
cards.back: Slower gastric secretion and emptying.

cards.front: What nerve supports cephalic stimulation of the stomach?
cards.back: Vagus nerve.

cards.front: What does the gastroileal reflex promote?
cards.back: Increased ileal movement toward the cecum with gastric activity.

cards.front: Gastrin: source and main effect?
cards.back: Gastric G cells; stimulates gastric acid/activity.

cards.front: Secretin: trigger and main effect?
cards.back: Duodenal acid; promotes pancreatic bicarbonate.

cards.front: CCK: trigger and main effects?
cards.back: Intestinal fats/proteins; pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction.

cards.front: Somatostatin: source and principal gastric effect?
cards.back: D cells; suppresses gastrin and acid.

cards.front: GIP: source and key effect?
cards.back: Intestinal K cells; glucose-dependent insulin stimulation.

cards.front: VIP: an important intestinal action?
cards.back: Vasodilation, with secretion-regulating effects.

cards.front: Which cells secrete CCK, secretin, and GIP?
cards.back: I cells, S cells, and K cells, respectively.

cards.front: Why do fat and acid tend to slow gastric emptying?
cards.back: Intestinal feedback limits delivery while the duodenum processes chyme.

cards.front: Name the three small-intestinal sections in order.
cards.back: Duodenum, jejunum, ileum.

cards.front: Which section receives bile and pancreatic secretions?
cards.back: Duodenum.

cards.front: Which section handles much of nutrient absorption?
cards.back: Jejunum.

cards.front: Which section reabsorbs bile salts and B12-intrinsic factor?
cards.back: Terminal ileum.

cards.front: Order intestinal surface structures from largest to smallest.
cards.back: Plicae circulares, villi, microvilli.

cards.front: Which structures receive chylomicrons?
cards.back: Intestinal lacteals.

cards.front: Where do glucose and amino acids usually go after absorption?
cards.back: Portal blood to the liver.

cards.front: What is the chylomicron route out of enterocytes?
cards.back: Enterocyte → lacteal → lymph → systemic blood.

cards.front: What do Brunner's glands secrete?
cards.back: Alkaline mucus in the duodenum.

cards.front: What do Paneth cells do?
cards.back: Release antimicrobial molecules in intestinal crypts.

cards.front: Where are Peyer's patches prominent?
cards.back: Ileum.

cards.front: What is the intestinal brush border?
cards.back: Enzyme-bearing microvilli on enterocytes.

cards.front: Identify pancreas head, body, and tail positions.
cards.back: Head in duodenal C-loop; body crosses abdomen; tail toward spleen.

cards.front: Exocrine acini versus endocrine islets?
cards.back: Acini secrete digestive enzymes; islets release hormones into blood.

cards.front: Which secretion neutralizes acidic chyme in the duodenum?
cards.back: Pancreatic bicarbonate-rich fluid.

cards.front: Which pancreatic enzyme attacks starch?
cards.back: Pancreatic amylase.

cards.front: Which pancreatic enzyme attacks triglycerides?
cards.back: Pancreatic lipase.

cards.front: Which pancreatic enzymes attack proteins?
cards.back: Proteases such as trypsin and chymotrypsin.

cards.front: Why is trypsinogen an inactive precursor?
cards.back: Protects the pancreas before intestinal activation.

cards.front: What is the duct of Wirsung?
cards.back: Main pancreatic duct.

cards.front: What is the difference between hepatocytes and Kupffer cells?
cards.back: Hepatocytes metabolize/produce bile; Kupffer cells are macrophages.

cards.front: Which organ makes bile, and which stores it?
cards.back: Liver makes; gallbladder stores and concentrates.

cards.front: Why is bile useful even though it has no digestive enzymes?
cards.back: It emulsifies lipids, aiding lipase access and absorption.

cards.front: How is the common hepatic duct formed?
cards.back: Right and left hepatic ducts unite.

cards.front: How is the common bile duct formed?
cards.back: Common hepatic duct joins cystic duct.

cards.front: Route of bile leaving a contracting gallbladder?
cards.back: Cystic duct → common bile duct → duodenum.

cards.front: Where does the biliary-pancreatic outflow usually enter the gut?
cards.back: Major duodenal papilla in descending duodenum.

cards.front: What does the sphincter of Oddi regulate?
cards.back: Entry of bile and pancreatic secretions into duodenum.

cards.front: Explain enterohepatic circulation in one line.
cards.back: Bile salts reabsorbed in ileum return via portal blood to liver.

cards.front: Which liver lobe is near the gallbladder fossa?
cards.back: Quadrate lobe.

cards.front: Which fetal vessel leaves the liver's round ligament?
cards.back: Umbilical vein.

cards.front: Name colon segments from cecum to rectum.
cards.back: Ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid, then rectum.

cards.front: Hepatic versus splenic flexure: where are they?
cards.back: Hepatic on right near liver; splenic on left near spleen.

cards.front: What are haustra and taeniae coli?
cards.back: Colon pouches and its longitudinal muscle bands.

cards.front: What initiates the defecation reflex?
cards.back: Rectal stretch from accumulating feces.

cards.front: Internal versus external anal sphincter: control?
cards.back: Internal involuntary smooth muscle; external voluntary skeletal muscle.

cards.front: Which colon process turns some fiber into absorbable fuel?
cards.back: Microbial fermentation to short-chain fatty acids.

cards.front: Which two main tasks does the colon perform?
cards.back: Recover water/electrolytes and compact/store feces.

cards.front: What are epiploic appendages?
cards.back: Small fat-filled serosal tags on colon.

cards.front: What is gastroesophageal reflux?
cards.back: Backflow of stomach contents into esophagus, often producing heartburn.

cards.front: Gastritis versus colitis?
cards.back: Stomach inflammation versus colon inflammation.

cards.front: What is pancreatitis?
cards.back: Inflammation of pancreas; sometimes linked to gallstone obstruction.

cards.front: What is cirrhosis?
cards.back: Advanced liver fibrosis and architectural distortion.

cards.front: What does jaundice indicate?
cards.back: Bilirubin-associated yellowing of skin or sclera.

cards.front: What is cholera's characteristic digestive effect?
cards.back: Profuse watery diarrhea from excessive intestinal fluid secretion.

cards.front: What is gingivitis?
cards.back: Inflammation of the gums.
